## Worldview
Medicine follows Galen and Avicenna: disease as imbalance of the four humours, plague from corrupted air (miasma) and unfavourable planetary conjunctions. Natural philosophy follows Aristotle (nature abhors a vacuum, four elements). Neoplatonism is fashionable at the Medici court (Ficino). Astrology is respected science. Workshops (botteghe), guilds, hospitals and the Studio at Pisa all train specialists. Florence is a republic in name, ruled in practice by Lorenzo de' Medici. Savonarola returns to San Marco in 1490.

## People
- **Lorenzo de' Medici ("il Magnifico")**: de-facto ruler of Florence, patron, poet; in poor health (gout). Knows: humanist learning, politics, banking. — Dies April 1492.
- **Marsilio Ficino**: Florentine priest, physician and translator of Plato, at the centre of a circle of humanists. Knows: Plato, astrology, Galenic medicine; wrote a treatise on plague (Consiglio contro la pestilenza).
- **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**: philosopher, prodigy, Medici circle.
- **Angelo Poliziano**: humanist, tutor of Lorenzo's children.
- **Girolamo Savonarola**: Dominican friar returning to San Marco in 1490. — His preaching attracts a growing following. He becomes prior in 1491.
- **Antonio Benivieni**: Florentine physician, early pioneer of autopsies to find causes of death.
- **Leonardo da Vinci**: engineer and artist at the Sforza court in Milan. Knows: hydraulics, mechanics, casting, anatomy. — Not in Florence – access requires travel to Milan.
- **Michelangelo Buonarroti**: teenage sculptor living in the Medici household (from c. 1490).
- **Luca Pacioli**: Franciscan mathematician from Sansepolcro, probably lecturing in Naples during the 1489–90 academic year.
- **Amerigo Vespucci**: Oversees household and estate business in Tuscany for Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici.
- **Pier Leoni da Spoleto**: Physician formerly at Pisa, in Rome in July and at Padua by November 1490. Knows: Galenic medicine and astrological prognosis, with links to Ficino and Poliziano. — Returns to treat Lorenzo in Florence by February 1492.
- **Niccolò Leoniceno**: physician and humanist, professor at Ferrara. Knows: Greek medical and botanical texts; checks Pliny and Avicenna against Dioscorides and Galen. — His criticism of medical errors in Pliny appears in Ferrara in 1492.
- **Alessandro Benedetti**: Physician from the Venetian territories with experience in Greece. Knows: Plague, surgery and anatomy. — His plague treatise appears in Venice in 1493. His whereabouts in 1490 and the claimed Padua chair are uncertain.
- **Luca Landucci**: apothecary with a shop at the Canto de' Tornaquinci; keeps a diary of city events. Knows: drugs, spices, sugar, wax, prices, city gossip. — His diary records prices and political and religious events in Florence.
- **Bertoldo di Giovanni**: sculptor, bronze caster and medallist; keeper of the Medici sculpture garden at San Marco. Knows: lost-wax casting, alloys, chasing; pupil of Donatello. — Dies at Poggio a Caiano in December 1491.
- **Andrea della Robbia**: head of the family workshop for tin-glazed terracotta sculpture (Via Guelfa). Knows: clays, kilns, tin and lead glazes, pigments; recipes kept in the family.
- **Bernardo Rucellai**: patrician, humanist, Lorenzo's brother-in-law. Knows: classical learning, politics; family fortune built on the orchil dye trade.
- **Francesco di Giorgio Martini**: Sienese architect and military engineer, serving Siena and the dukes of Urbino and Calabria. Knows: pumps, mills, cranes, fortification, gunpowder mines; his illustrated treatises circulate in manuscript. — Consulted in Milan in 1490, he travels with Leonardo to Pavia in June to advise on the cathedral.
- **Lorenzo della Volpaia**: Florentine clockmaker and instrument maker. Knows: gear trains, tower and chamber clocks, astronomical instruments. — Designs planetary clocks for Medici patrons.
- **Giuliano da Sangallo**: Florentine architect, woodworker and military engineer, favoured by Lorenzo de' Medici. Knows: building machines, fortification, ancient architecture, timber and models. — Builds the villa at Poggio a Caiano. A route to Lorenzo for anything concerning building.
- **Bonaccorso Ghiberti**: Florentine bronze founder and engineer, grandson of Lorenzo Ghiberti. Knows: bell and gun founding; keeps a notebook (Zibaldone) with drawings of Brunelleschi's hoists.
- **Filippo Calandri**: Florentine abacus master. Knows: commercial arithmetic, long division, rule of three. — His printed arithmetic (Florence, 1 January 1491 Florentine style, i.e. 1492) is dedicated to the young Giuliano de' Medici.
- **Piero della Francesca**: Painter and mathematician in Borgo San Sepolcro. Knows: perspective, Euclid, Archimedes, the regular solids, abacus arithmetic. — Dies 12 October 1492. Luca Pacioli comes from the same town.
- **Domenico Maria Novara**: professor of astronomy at Bologna, issues yearly astrological forecasts. Knows: Ptolemy, observation, tables; doubts some of Ptolemy's values. — Copernicus studies with him in Bologna from 1496.
- **Franchino Gaffurio**: choirmaster of Milan cathedral and music theorist. Knows: string ratios, tuning, Pythagorean and Boethian theory of sound.
- **Henricus Martellus Germanus**: German mapmaker working in Florence (c. 1480–96). Knows: Ptolemy's maps, portolan charts; his world maps of c. 1489–91 already show Africa's southern tip from Portuguese reports of Dias. — His maps show that reports of Portuguese discoveries already circulate in Florence.
- **Francesco Rosselli**: Florentine miniaturist, engraver and map seller. Knows: copper engraving, printing of maps, the map trade. — His engraved maps and prints offer a Florentine route to reproducing a new chart.
- **Giorgio Antonio Vespucci**: humanist cleric and teacher, uncle and tutor of Amerigo; close to Ficino and to San Marco. Knows: Latin and Greek, cosmography, owns and copies manuscripts. — Way into the Vespucci family and to Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco.
- **Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici**: head of the junior Medici branch, rich, on poor terms with Lorenzo il Magnifico's line; employer of Amerigo Vespucci. Knows: trade with Spain, patronage (Botticelli). — His household has business connections in Seville through the Niccolini.
- **Giannotto (Juanoto) Berardi**: Florentine merchant in Seville, active in the slave trade and linked to Marchionni in Lisbon. Knows: Castilian court finance, fitting out ships in Andalusia. — Vespucci is documented with him in 1492. Berardi finances Columbus and supplies later voyages, then dies in 1495.
- **Bartolomeo Marchionni**: Florentine merchant-banker in Lisbon, among the richest men in Portugal. Knows: Atlantic commerce, including the trade in enslaved Africans, and credit to the Portuguese crown. — Helped finance the overland mission of Pêro da Covilhã and Afonso de Paiva, who departed in 1487.
- **Cristoforo Colombo (Columbus)**: Genoese mariner seeking Castilian royal support for a westward voyage to Asia. Knows: Atlantic navigation and the westward-route proposal associated with Toscanelli. — He puts Japan much too close to the Canaries. Some reconstructions give about 2,400 nautical miles. Royal approval comes in April 1492.
- **João II of Portugal**: King of Portugal, patron of voyages along the African coast. Knows: Reports from Dias's expedition and astronomical observations commissioned from José Vizinho. — He had declined Columbus's westward proposal in the 1480s.
- **José Vizinho**: Physician and astronomer in Portuguese royal service. Knows: Solar altitudes on the Guinea coast, which he observed for João II in 1485.
- **Bartolomeu Dias**: Portuguese captain, returned to Lisbon in December 1488 after rounding the Cape. Knows: The passage around southern Africa and part of its Indian Ocean coast. — Vasco da Gama's fleet sails for India in 1497.
- **Abraham Zacuto**: Jewish astronomer in Castile, under the patronage of Juan de Zúñiga. Knows: astronomical tables including the sun's declination (his Hebrew tables of the 1470s). — Documented in Lisbon in 1493 after the expulsion. José Vizinho's Latin version of his tables is printed at Leiria in 1496.
- **Martin Behaim**: Nuremberg merchant who lived in Lisbon and the Azores; back in Nuremberg 1490–93. Knows: Atlantic merchant routes and reports of Portuguese exploration. — Nuremberg commissions his terrestrial globe around 1492. No American mainland appears on it.
- **Bartolomeo Scala**: chancellor of Florence. Knows: diplomacy, law, the workings of every council.
- **Niccolò Machiavelli**: young Florentine of 21 from a modest lawyer's family, without office. Knows: Latin historians. — His documented Florentine government service begins in 1498.

## Events and timeline
- 1488 Dec (background): Dias returns to Lisbon after rounding southern Africa. News reaches mapmakers in Florence.
- 1490: Regiomontanus' Tabulae directionum (with a tangent table) printed at Augsburg
- 1490 Jun: Leonardo and Francesco di Giorgio Martini travel together from Milan to Pavia to advise on the cathedral
- 1490 Aug: After returning to Florence, Savonarola begins a series of sermons at San Marco.
- 1490: Mercury is discovered at Idrija in Carniola. Almadén is already an established source.
- c. 1490: Columbus continues seeking Castilian backing. Advisers examining the proposed westward route doubt its feasibility.
- 1490: Maximilian I hires the Tassis family to run a relay post from Innsbruck to the Netherlands
- 1490: the first printed portolano (sailing directions) appears in Venice
- c. 1490–91: Pêro da Covilhã returns to Cairo with information on Indian Ocean trade. Whether his report reached João II is uncertain.
- 1491: The illustrated Fasciculus medicinae appears in Venice. An expanded Italian edition follows in 1494.
- 1491 Nov–1492 Mar: Amerigo Vespucci moves from Florence to Seville. He is a witness there on 10 March 1492.
- 1491 Dec: Bertoldo di Giovanni dies at Poggio a Caiano
- 1492 Jan 1: Filippo Calandri's illustrated arithmetic is printed in Florence, with worked examples of long division.
- 1492 Jan 2: Granada surrenders to Castile; Apr 17: the Capitulations of Santa Fe grant Columbus his voyage
- 1492 Apr 5: lightning strikes the lantern of the Duomo and marble crashes down, three days before Lorenzo's death; taken as an omen
- 1492 Apr 8: Lorenzo de' Medici dies at Careggi. His son Piero succeeds him.
- 1492 Apr 9: Pier Leoni is found dead in a well near Careggi. Contemporary accounts disagree about the circumstances.
- 1492: Niccolò Leoniceno prints his attack on Pliny's errors in medicine (Ferrara); a public quarrel among humanists follows
- 1492 Mar–Jul: Jews are expelled from Spain; many skilled refugees reach Portugal and Italy
- c. 1492: Behaim and Nuremberg craftsmen make a terrestrial globe for the city council.
- 1492 Jul–Aug: Innocent VIII dies and Alexander VI is elected. A hostile rumour about three boys' blood later becomes a transfusion legend.
- 1492 Aug 3: Columbus sails from Palos with three ships; Oct 12: landfall in the Bahamas
- 1492 Sep: At sea Columbus records a change in the compass bearing of Polaris.
- 1492 Oct 12: Piero della Francesca dies in Sansepolcro
- 1493 Mar–Oct: Columbus returns via Lisbon to Palos with captives. His letter appears in Barcelona, in Latin in Rome, and in Italian verse in Rome and Florence.
- 1493 May: Alexander VI's Inter caetera grants the Castilian monarchs a claim to lands west of an Atlantic line, subject to exceptions for existing Christian rulers.
- 1493 Sep: Columbus's second fleet of seventeen ships sails from Cádiz.
- 1493 Nov: Leonardo's full-size clay model of the Sforza horse is shown in Milan; in 1494 its bronze goes to Ferrara for cannon
- 1494 Jun: Castile and Portugal agree at Tordesillas on a demarcation line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands.
- 1494 Sep–Nov: Charles VIII crosses the Alps with a mobile siege train; the Florentine fortress of Fivizzano is stormed and its garrison killed; Piero de' Medici hands over Sarzana, Pietrasanta, Pisa and Livorno
- 1494 Nov: Pacioli's Summa appears in Venice. It discusses cubic equations and gives a disputed rule for dividing stakes in an interrupted game.
- 1494 Nov–Dec: Pisa rebels, the Medici are expelled and Charles VIII enters Florence. A new Great Council is established in December.
- 1494–95: A major outbreak of the disease later called syphilis is associated with the Naples campaign.
- Recurring: plague outbreaks (the city still remembers 1478–79)
- Recurring: floods of the Arno, bad harvests, grain shortages
- Every summer: tertian and quartan fevers in the Pisan plain and Maremma; fluxes in the city

## Quest hooks
- Lorenzo's gout and pain – relief brings access to the Medici court
- A plague outbreak in a poor quarter (San Frediano, Santo Spirito)
- Mine owners need water pumped from deep shafts
- The Signoria wants faster news from Pisa and Livorno
- A glassblower or spectacle maker looking for a new product
- Merchants who want easier calculation and better accounts
- Making the trip to Milan to meet Leonardo
- Midwives in one parish report several deaths after childbirth. A physician at Santa Maria Nuova offers to compare their accounts.
- A dyer of the Arte della Lana wants a bleach or colour nobody else has
- A gilder with trembling hands and loose teeth, and a workshop full of mercury fumes
- Lorenzo's model farm at Poggio a Caiano is open to new crops, stock and methods
- A landlord's wine turns to vinegar every August
- Fetching a glassmaker from Murano, or brass and crucibles from the German lands
- A Pisan landowner wants water for a rice field. Neighbours on the marshy plain already complain of summer fevers.
- The chancery suspects that Milan reads its ciphered letters and wants a cipher nobody can break
- A Florentine clockmaker wants to compare a new regulator with Lorenzo della Volpaia's work.
- An abacus master posts a public challenge with a cubic equation and a purse for the solver
- The Opera del Duomo wants to protect the lantern after yet another lightning strike
- The mint has tested a suspect payment by touchstone. Can weighing the coins in water give the assayers a second check?
- A gun founder's bombard has burst and killed its crew; the Signoria wants an account of what happened
- A silk merchant wants to know how Bologna's water-driven throwing mills work
- An astrologer needs tedious multiplications of sines done faster for the next year's almanac
- A Florentine house with partners in Lisbon and Seville wants to know what a westward voyage to the spice markets would cost.
- A reader of Toscanelli's westward proposal asks the player to check how far apart the Canaries and Japan really are.
- Martellus's map shows Africa's southern tip. A visitor asks how much of the new coastline can be trusted.
- A merchant can book passage from Livorno on a Genoese ship. Winds and scheduled stops will determine when the player reaches Iberia.
- A Florentine banker in Lisbon offers introductions to merchants who have heard Dias's report.
- A Portuguese pilot wants an easier way to take an altitude on a rolling deck and check the result against observations ashore.
- A crew returning from Guinea reports swollen gums after a long passage. The victualler wants provisions that will keep.
- The Otto di Pratica hear rumours of the French king's guns and ask whether Sarzana's new walls would stand
- A broker at the Mercato Nuovo wants to price insurance on an untried route.
- Rival physicians or guild officers challenge the player over a treatment, a lost possession or an accusation of sorcery.
